steps: Step 1, Control the tense by matching it to the time clue. Finished time uses the past simple: I lived in Cairo in 2015. Time that continues to now uses the present perfect: I have lived here since 2019. Ask first: does the time word say 'finished' (yesterday, in 2015) or 'up to now' (since, for)?

Step 2, Add the past perfect for the earlier of two past events. When I arrived, the train had left. The leaving happened first, so it takes had plus the past participle. Compare: When I arrived, the train left (it left after I came). Write two pairs of sentences and say which event came first.

Step 3, Control articles. Use a or an for one of many: She is a doctor. Use the for something known or unique: The doctor I met was kind. Use no article for general plural or abstract ideas: Doctors work hard. Life is short. Also say She plays the piano and I go to school by bus.

Step 4, Control prepositions with fixed patterns. Time: at six o'clock, on Monday, in July. Adjective plus preposition: good at maths, interested in music, afraid of dogs. Verb plus preposition: depend on, wait for, listen to. Learn them as whole chunks and test yourself by covering the preposition.

Step 5, Edit a paragraph with three types of error. Wrong: Yesterday I have gone to market on the Monday. I am interested on fruit. Right: Yesterday I went to the market. I am interested in fruit. The errors were a tense (yesterday needs the past simple), an article (the market) and a preposition (interested in). Check each type separately.

Step 6, Your turn: correct this sentence. I am living here since three years and my sister is good in maths and plays piano. Answer: I have lived here for three years and my sister is good at maths and plays the piano.

Step 1, Read the whole text once for the general idea. Je m'appelle Nora. J'ai neuf ans. J'habite à Lyon avec ma mère, mon père et mon chat. Le matin, je vais à l'école à pied. J'aime lire et dessiner. Le mercredi, je joue au tennis. Ask: who is speaking, and about what? [Nora, about herself.]

Step 2, Work out the meaning line by line. J'habite [I live], avec ma mère [with my mother], le matin [in the morning], à pied [on foot], j'aime lire [I like reading], le mercredi [on Wednesdays]. Underline words that look like English, such as tennis, and words you already know, such as chat and école.

Step 3, Learn the question words. Qui ? [Who?] Où ? [Where?] Quand ? [When?] Quel âge ? [How old?] Que fait-elle ? [What does she do?] Match: Où habite Nora ? Look for habite in the text, then answer: Elle habite à Lyon. [She lives in Lyon.]

Step 4, Answer in a full sentence. Quel âge a Nora ? [How old is Nora?] Nora a neuf ans. [Nora is nine.] Avec qui habite-t-elle ? [Who does she live with?] Elle habite avec sa mère, son père et son chat. Change je to elle and ma to sa when you copy.

Step 5, Fix common errors. A child writes Nora habite à Paris without checking the text. Correction: Nora habite à Lyon, so always find the proof. Another says Elle joue au tennis le lundi. Correction: le mercredi. A third writes Je habite; say J'habite.

Step 6, Your turn: read Hugo a dix ans. Il habite à Marseille avec sa sœur. Le samedi, il joue au football. Answer the question Que fait Hugo le samedi ? Answer: Il joue au football le samedi. [He plays football on Saturdays.]

Step 1, Start with a sentence frame. Je m'appelle Samir. J'ai neuf ans. J'habite dans une grande ville. [My name is Samir. I am nine. I live in a big city.] Copy the frame and put your own name, age and place in it. Begin each sentence with a capital letter and end with a full stop.

Step 2, Add family and pets. J'ai un frère et une sœur. [I have a brother and a sister.] J'ai un chien. Il s'appelle Max. [I have a dog. His name is Max.] Use J'ai, not Je suis, for age, brothers, sisters and pets. Write two sentences about your own family.

Step 3, Say what you like. J'aime le football et j'aime lire. [I like football and I like reading.] Je n'aime pas les araignées. [I do not like spiders.] Join ideas with et [and] and mais [but]: J'aime la pizza, mais je n'aime pas le poisson. [I like pizza, but I do not like fish.]

Step 4, Put the text together and check it. Write six sentences in order: name, age, town, family, pet, likes. Check capitals, full stops and accents such as école, frère and très. Read it aloud once and listen for a sentence that sounds wrong.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes Je suis neuf ans. Correction: J'ai neuf ans. Another writes mon sœur. Correction: ma sœur, because sœur is feminine. Another writes frere without the accent. Correction: frère, with the grave accent.

Step 6, Your turn: write four sentences about you with name, age, one like and one pet. Model answer: Je m'appelle Lina. J'ai dix ans. J'aime dessiner. J'ai un chat et il s'appelle Mimi. [My name is Lina. I am ten. I like drawing. I have a cat and his name is Mimi.]

Step 1, Prepare before listening. An adult reads the dialogue aloud twice (script in Step 2). Predict first: the title is À la boulangerie [At the bakery]. Which words might you hear? Likely pain [bread], croissant, s'il vous plaît [please], euro and some numbers. Write them down.

Step 2, Listen once for the gist. Read aloud: Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais deux croissants et une baguette, s'il vous plaît. Voilà. Un croissant coûte un euro vingt et la baguette un euro. Ça fait combien ? Trois euros quarante. Merci, au revoir ! [Hello. I would like two croissants and a baguette, please. Here you are. A croissant costs 1.20 and the baguette 1.00. How much is that? 3.40. Thank you, goodbye!] Gist: buying bread.

Step 3, Listen again for details. Note: deux croissants [2], une baguette [1], un euro vingt [1.20 each], un euro [1.00 for the baguette]. Write the numbers as figures, not words. Stop the reader after each price if you need more time.

Step 4, Check the answer by calculating. 2 x 1.20 = 2.40 and 2.40 + 1.00 = 3.40. The shopkeeper said trois euros quarante, so what you heard matches your sum. If it does not match, listen again for the number you missed.

Step 5, Fix common listening slips. Deux [2] and dix [10] sound different: deux ends with an open sound, dix with an s sound. Un euro vingt means 1.20, not 20 euros. Quarante [40] and quatorze [14] begin alike, so listen to the end of the word.
Step 6, Your turn: hear Je voudrais trois pommes. Une pomme coûte soixante centimes. Ça fait combien ? Answer: 3 x 0.60 = 1.80, so Ça fait un euro quatre-vingts. [That makes 1.80.]

Step 1, Choose a simple topic and plan four points. Topic: mon chat [my cat]. Points: name, looks, likes, how I feel. Write one keyword for each point on a small card: nom, petit et noir, dormir, je l'aime. The card helps you remember without reading every word.

Step 2, Build one sentence per point. Il s'appelle Pixel. [His name is Pixel.] Il est petit et noir. [He is small and black.] Il aime dormir et jouer avec une balle. [He likes sleeping and playing with a ball.] Je l'aime beaucoup. [I love him very much.]

Step 3, Add a start and an end. Start: Bonjour ! Je vais parler de mon chat. [Hello! I am going to talk about my cat.] End: Merci de m'écouter ! [Thank you for listening!] Your whole talk is now six short sentences, about 40 words.

Step 4, Practise the sounds. Say each sentence slowly. The s at the end of petits is silent. In beaucoup say bo-koo. Say the talk three times: once to a mirror, once to a toy, once to a friend. Speak loudly, slowly and look up at the end of each sentence.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child says Il s'appelle est Pixel. Correction: Il s'appelle Pixel. Another says Il a petit. Correction: Il est petit, because we use est with an adjective. A third says Il a aime jouer. Correction: Il aime jouer, with only one verb.

Step 6, Your turn: give a four-sentence talk about your family. Model answer: Bonjour ! Je vais parler de ma famille. J'ai une sœur et un frère. Ma sœur s'appelle Rima et mon frère s'appelle Adam. Merci de m'écouter ! [Hello! I am going to talk about my family. I have a sister and a brother. My sister is Rima and my brother is Adam. Thank you for listening!]

Step 1, Skim the text for the main idea. Samedi, Amir et sa sœur Lina vont au marché avec leur grand-père. Ils achètent des tomates, du fromage et une baguette. Il pleut, alors ils rentrent vite à la maison. L'après-midi, ils font un gâteau au chocolat. Main idea: a Saturday outing and baking at home.

Step 2, Read for details and gloss new words. ils vont [they go], ils achètent [they buy], il pleut [it is raining], alors [so], rentrer [to go back home], l'après-midi [in the afternoon], un gâteau [a cake]. Underline the verbs, because question answers usually depend on them.

Step 3, Identify what each question word asks for. Qui ? [Who?] gives a person. Où ? [Where?] gives a place. Quand ? [When?] gives a time. Pourquoi ? [Why?] needs parce que [because]. Combien ? [How many?] needs a number. Read the question before you hunt in the text.

Step 4, Find the evidence and write the answer. Où vont-ils samedi ? [Where do they go on Saturday?] Evidence: vont au marché. Answer: Ils vont au marché avec leur grand-père. [They go to the market with their grandfather.] Reuse words from the question and the text, changing only what is needed.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child answers Pourquoi rentrent-ils vite ? with Il pleut. Better: Ils rentrent vite parce qu'il pleut. Another answers Ils achètent du fromage et pain. Correction: du fromage et une baguette, as in the text. Always check the text before you copy.
Step 6, Your turn: answer Que font-ils l'après-midi ? [What do they do in the afternoon?] Answer: Ils font un gâteau au chocolat. [They make a chocolate cake.]

Step 1, Begin with a topic sentence that names the subject. Le samedi, je me lève à huit heures. [On Saturdays I get up at eight.] Note je me lève, not je lève, because se lever is a reflexive verb. Every other sentence in the paragraph will support this opening.

Step 2, Add sequence words. d'abord [first], ensuite [then], puis [next], enfin [finally]. D'abord, je prends le petit déjeuner. [First, I have breakfast.] Ensuite, je joue au foot avec mes amis. [Then I play football with my friends.] Use a comma after each sequence word.

Step 3, Write the middle and the end. Puis, je fais mes devoirs. [Next, I do my homework.] Enfin, le soir, je regarde un film avec ma famille. [Finally, in the evening, I watch a film with my family.] That gives five sentences, a good length for a paragraph.

Step 4, Check the paragraph. Verbs in the present: je me lève, je prends, je joue, je fais, je regarde. Accents: élève, devoirs, film. Check that every sentence begins with a capital and ends with a full stop. Read aloud and fix anything that sounds odd.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes Je joue le foot. Correction: Je joue au foot, because jouer takes à before a sport. Another writes je lève à huit heures. Correction: je me lève à huit heures. Another writes Je fait mes devoirs. Correction: Je fais.

Step 6, Your turn: write four or five sentences about your Sunday with sequence words. Model answer: Le dimanche, je dors un peu plus. D'abord, je mange avec mes parents. Ensuite, je lis un livre. Puis, je joue avec mon frère. Enfin, je prépare mon sac.

Step 1, Prepare to listen. The title is Pour aller à la gare [Getting to the station]. Predict words: tout droit [straight on], à gauche [on the left], à droite [on the right], la rue [street], mètres [metres]. Draw a small blank map with the start point marked.

Step 2, Listen for the gist. Read aloud: Excusez-moi, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ? Allez tout droit jusqu'au feu rouge, puis tournez à gauche. Ensuite, prenez la deuxième rue à droite. La gare est en face de la poste. C'est loin ? Non, c'est à cinq cents mètres. Gist: someone asks the way to the station.

Step 3, Listen again and draw the route. Straight to the red light [le feu rouge], left, then the second street on the right. The station is opposite [en face de] the post office [la poste]. Mark each step with an arrow as you hear it.

Step 4, Check the numbers and the detail. cinq cents mètres is 500 m. At about 5 km per hour, 500 m takes six minutes, so sept minutes à pied [seven minutes on foot] is reasonable. Compare your map with a partner's and listen again where they differ.

Step 5, Fix common slips. À gauche [left] and à droite [right] are easy to swap, so write G and D. Tout droit means straight on, not to the right. Cent [100] and cinq cents [500] differ by cinq, so listen for it. Say them aloud.

Step 6, Your turn: hear Allez tout droit, puis tournez à droite. La bibliothèque est à côté de la pharmacie, à trois cents mètres. Where is it and how far? Answer: It is next to the pharmacy, after turning right, 300 metres away.

Step 1, Learn greetings and first questions. Salut ! Comment tu t'appelles ? [Hi! What is your name?] Tu as quel âge ? [How old are you?] Tu habites où ? [Where do you live?] Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ? [What do you like to do?] Practise each with a partner, turn by turn.

Step 2, Answer in a full sentence and return the question. Je m'appelle Yara. Et toi ? [My name is Yara. And you?] J'ai onze ans. Et toi ? [I am eleven. And you?] Et toi ? keeps the conversation going and gives you time to think.

Step 3, Act out a conversation. Paul : Tu habites où ? [Where do you live?] Yara : J'habite près du parc. [I live near the park.] Paul : Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ? Yara : J'aime nager et lire. Et toi ? Paul : J'adore le foot ! Yara : Super ! [Great!]

Step 4, Add small words to sound natural. Euh [Um], alors [so], bien sûr [of course], d'accord [OK], pardon ? [Sorry?]. If you do not hear, say Tu peux répéter, s'il te plaît ? [Can you repeat, please?] Use one of these in every conversation.
Step 5, Fix errors. A child says Je habite près du parc. Correction: J'habite, with elision before the h. Another says Tu habites quoi ? Correction: Tu habites où ?

Step 6, Your turn: have a six-line conversation about hobbies with a partner. Model answer: Salut ! Tu aimes faire quoi ? J'aime dessiner. Et toi ? Moi, j'aime jouer au basket. Super ! On joue samedi ? D'accord ! [Hi! What do you like to do? I like drawing. And you? I like playing basketball. Great! Shall we play on Saturday? OK!]

Step 1, Read the text once, then again. Hier, Clara est allée à la piscine avec sa cousine. Elles ont nagé pendant une heure, puis elles ont mangé une glace. Clara n'a pas pris son bonnet, alors le maître nageur lui a prêté un bonnet. [Yesterday Clara went to the pool with her cousin. They swam for an hour, then ate an ice cream. Clara did not take her cap, so the lifeguard lent her one.]

Step 2, Spot the tense and the helper verb. Aller uses être: Clara est allée. Nager and manger use avoir: elles ont nagé, elles ont mangé. These are the passé composé, for finished past actions. Underline each helper verb and its past participle before you answer.

Step 3, Turn the question into the start of your answer. Où est allée Clara ? becomes Clara est allée à la piscine. Qu'est-ce qu'elles ont mangé ? becomes Elles ont mangé une glace. Reuse the same helper verb and past participle as the question.

Step 4, Give reasons in full. Pourquoi le maître nageur a-t-il prêté un bonnet à Clara ? [Why did the lifeguard lend Clara a cap?] Answer in a full sentence: Le maître nageur a prêté un bonnet à Clara parce qu'elle n'a pas pris le sien. Do not answer with only Parce que.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes Clara est allé. Correction: allée, because être verbs agree with the subject and Clara is feminine. Another writes Elles ont allé. Correction: Elles sont allées. Another writes Clara a pas pris. Correction: Clara n'a pas pris, with ne and pas around a.
Step 6, Your turn: answer Combien de temps ont-elles nagé ? [How long did they swim?] Answer: Elles ont nagé pendant une heure. [They swam for an hour.]

Step 1, Plan a short letter in four parts: greeting, about me, last weekend, a question. Open with Chère Zoé, for a girl or Cher Zoé, for a boy. Close with À bientôt or Amitiés. Write the plan as four bullets before you start the full text.

Step 2, Write the opening and the present tense. Chère Zoé, merci pour ta lettre. Je m'appelle Ibrahim et j'ai douze ans. J'habite dans un appartement près d'un parc. [Dear Zoé, thank you for your letter. My name is Ibrahim and I am twelve. I live in a flat near a park.]

Step 3, Add the past with the passé composé. Le week-end dernier, j'ai joué au basket et j'ai visité un musée avec mon père. [Last weekend I played basketball and visited a museum with my father.] Both verbs use avoir plus the past participle: joué, visité.

Step 4, Close with a question and a sign-off. Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ? Écris-moi vite ! [And you, what do you like to do? Write to me soon!] Amitiés, Ibrahim. Count about 55 words. Read the letter aloud and check each verb.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes J'ai allé au musée. Correction: Je suis allé au musée, because aller takes être. Another writes Cher Zoé to a girl. Correction: Chère Zoé. A third writes j'ai joue. Correction: j'ai joué, with the é ending.

Step 6, Your turn: write three sentences about last weekend using the passé composé. Model answer: Samedi dernier, j'ai regardé un film. Dimanche, je suis allée chez ma grand-mère. J'ai mangé un bon gâteau. [Last Saturday I watched a film. On Sunday I went to my grandmother's. I ate a good cake.]

Step 1, Predict before listening. The title is On organise samedi [Planning Saturday]. Expect times, activities and a decision. Draw a three-column table: Qui [who], Quand [when], Quoi [what]. Decide to listen twice: once for the gist, once for the details.

Step 2, Listen for the gist. Read aloud: Léa : Tu es libre samedi ? Tom : Le matin, j'ai un cours de guitare jusqu'à onze heures, mais l'après-midi, je suis libre. Léa : On pourrait aller au cinéma à quinze heures trente. Tom : Bonne idée ! Le film dure combien de temps ? Léa : Une heure quarante. Tom : Alors on sort à dix-sept heures dix. On mange une crêpe après ? Léa : D'accord ! Gist: two friends plan an outing.

Step 3, Fill the table on the second listening. Qui : Léa and Tom. Quand : samedi, 15 h 30 (quinze heures trente). Quoi : cinéma, then une crêpe [a pancake]. Also note Tom's guitar lesson until 11 h (onze heures) and that the film lasts 1 h 40.

Step 4, Check an inference with a calculation. 15 h 30 plus 1 h 40 equals 17 h 10. Tom says dix-sept heures dix, which is correct. When a speaker gives a start time and a length, work out the end time yourself and compare with what you hear.

Step 5, Fix common slips. French often uses the 24-hour clock in speech: quinze heures trente is 3.30 p.m. Do not confuse quinze [15] with quarante [40] or dix-sept [17] with dix-huit [18]. Un quart d'heure [quarter of an hour] is different from quatorze heures [2 p.m.].

Step 6, Your turn: hear Le cours commence à neuf heures quarante-cinq et dure une heure trente. À quelle heure finit-il ? Answer: 9 h 45 plus 1 h 30 is 11 h 15, so il finit à onze heures quinze. [It ends at 11.15.]

Step 1, Pick a topic and a plan. Topic: mon quartier [my neighbourhood]. Plan: introduce, location, what there is, what I like, conclude. A one-minute talk for a language learner at a careful pace is about 60 to 80 words, so about eight to ten short sentences.

Step 2, Build the introduction and location. Bonjour à tous. Je vais vous présenter mon quartier. [Hello everyone. I am going to present my neighbourhood.] D'abord, il est situé près d'un grand parc. [First, it is near a big park.] Je vais plus infinitive is the near future.

Step 3, Add the middle and the opinion. Ensuite, il y a une bibliothèque, un petit marché et deux écoles. [Then there is a library, a small market and two schools.] Enfin, ce que j'aime, c'est le calme et mes amis. [Finally, what I like is the calm and my friends.]

Step 4, Close and deliver. Pour conclure, mon quartier est petit mais agréable. Merci de m'écouter. [To conclude, my neighbourhood is small but pleasant. Thank you for listening.] Use cue cards with one keyword each, look at the audience, and pause for a breath after each sequence word.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child says Je vais présente. Correction: Je vais présenter, because after aller we use the infinitive. Another says il y a un bibliothèque. Correction: une bibliothèque, because it is feminine. Another reads every word; use keywords instead.

Step 6, Your turn: present your school in five sentences. Model answer: Bonjour à tous. Je vais vous présenter mon école. D'abord, elle est près de ma maison. Ensuite, il y a une grande cour et un gymnase. Pour conclure, j'aime mon école parce que mes amis sont là. Merci !

Step 1, Collect facts in two columns. In France: école primaire five years (ages 6 to 11), collège four years (11 to 15), lycée three years (15 to 18), ending with the baccalauréat. For comparison use an invented system B: six years of primary, three of lower secondary, three of upper secondary. Total in both: 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 and 6 + 3 + 3 = 12.

Step 2, Learn the comparison forms. plus ... que [more ... than], moins ... que [less ... than], aussi ... que [as ... as]. Le primaire est plus long dans le système B qu'en France. [Primary school is longer in system B than in France.] Les deux systèmes durent aussi longtemps. [Both systems last as long.]

Step 3, Link ideas with contrast words. alors que, tandis que [whereas], par contre [on the other hand], en revanche [in contrast]. En France, le collège dure quatre ans, alors que dans le système B le premier cycle du secondaire dure trois ans. [In France lower secondary lasts four years, whereas in system B it lasts three.]

Step 4, Add a similarity and an opinion. Dans les deux systèmes, les élèves passent douze ans à l'école. [In both systems, pupils spend twelve years at school.] À mon avis, un collège plus long permet de mieux préparer le lycée. [In my opinion a longer collège prepares better for lycée.]

Step 5, Fix errors. A child says plus bon. Correction: meilleur, since bon has an irregular comparative. Another says aussi long comme. Correction: aussi long que. Another writes Le système est plus longue. Correction: plus long, because système is masculine. Check agreement.

Step 6, Your turn: compare country A with five school days of 8 hours and country B with four school days of 8 hours. Answer: Dans le pays A, les élèves sont à l'école 40 heures par semaine, alors que dans le pays B ils y sont 32 heures. La semaine est donc plus longue dans le pays A.

Step 1, Locate French-speaking places. French is spoken by more than 300 million people on five continents. Countries with French as an official language include la France, la Belgique, la Suisse, le Canada, le Sénégal and la Côte d'Ivoire. Use en with feminine countries and au with masculine ones: en France, au Canada, au Sénégal.

Step 2, Describe languages and everyday facts. La Suisse a quatre langues nationales : l'allemand, le français, l'italien et le romanche. [Switzerland has four national languages.] Au Québec, la langue officielle est le français. [In Quebec, the official language is French.] Use est and a to give facts.

Step 3, Describe festivals and food. En France, la fête nationale est le 14 juillet. [In France the national day is 14 July.] Au Québec, la fête nationale est le 24 juin. En Belgique, on mange des frites et des gaufres. En Suisse, on mange de la fondue. Au Québec, on mange de la poutine.

Step 4, Write a short description. Au Sénégal, le français est une langue officielle, mais beaucoup de gens parlent aussi le wolof. [In Senegal French is an official language, but many people also speak Wolof.] Use on and il y a to describe general customs without needing exact names.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes Je vais en Canada. Correction: au Canada. Another says La Suisse a trois langues. Correction: quatre. Another uses capital letters: Français, Juillet. Correction: le français is a language and juillet a month, both written with small letters.

Step 6, Your turn: describe one French-speaking country in three sentences. Model answer: La Belgique est un pays en Europe. On y parle français, néerlandais et allemand. On y mange des frites et des gaufres. [Belgium is a country in Europe. French, Dutch and German are spoken there. People eat chips and waffles there.]

Step 1, Skim the text and name the topic. Depuis septembre, les élèves de notre lycée participent à un projet pour réduire les déchets. Chaque classe trie le papier, le plastique et les restes de repas. Avant le projet, le lycée produisait 800 kilos de déchets par semaine. Aujourd'hui, il en produit 120 de moins, soit une baisse de 15 %. Le directeur espère atteindre 25 % de réduction avant juin, mais certains élèves pensent que ce sera difficile parce que la cantine jette encore trop de pain.

Step 2, Analyse the question before you search. Depuis quand le projet existe-t-il ? [Since when has the project existed?] Depuis quand asks for a starting point in time. Evidence: depuis septembre. Reuse the question's words: Le projet existe depuis septembre. [The project has existed since September.]

Step 3, Combine information to answer an inference question. Combien de kilos de déchets le lycée produit-il maintenant par semaine ? The text gives 800 before and 120 fewer now, so 800 - 120 = 680. Check the percentage: 120 / 800 = 0.15, which is 15 %. Answer: Le lycée produit maintenant 680 kilos de déchets par semaine.

Step 4, Explain a reason with evidence. Pourquoi certains élèves pensent-ils que l'objectif sera difficile ? [Why do some pupils think the target will be difficult?] Answer: Ils pensent que ce sera difficile parce que la cantine jette encore trop de pain. Quote the cause and keep ce sera as in the text.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child answers 680 kilos without a sentence. Correction: give a full sentence with a verb. Another confuses 15 % of 800 with 15 kilos. Correction: 15 % of 800 is 120. Another writes Ils produisent for the lycée; use Il produit, singular.

Step 6, Your turn: by how many kilos must weekly waste fall further to reach the director's 25 % target? Answer: 25 % of 800 is 200, so the target is 600 kilos; 680 - 600 = 80. Il faut encore réduire les déchets de 80 kilos par semaine.

Step 1, Analyse the essay question and take a position. Faut-il interdire les téléphones portables au lycée ? [Should mobile phones be banned at school?] Choose a clear thesis: they should be banned during lessons but allowed at break. Write one sentence thesis, then two arguments and one counter-argument.

Step 2, Write an introduction in three moves. Aujourd'hui, presque tous les lycéens ont un téléphone portable. [Today nearly all pupils have a mobile.] Faut-il pour autant l'interdire en classe ? [Should it therefore be banned in class?] Nous verrons d'abord que le téléphone gêne l'apprentissage, puis qu'il reste un outil utile. [We shall see first that ... then that ...]

Step 3, Develop argument and example. Tout d'abord, un téléphone qui sonne distrait toute la classe. [First, a phone that rings distracts the whole class.] Par exemple, un élève qui lit ses messages ne suit plus le cours. [For example, a pupil reading messages no longer follows the lesson.] Each paragraph needs one claim and one example.

Step 4, Add a counter-argument and a conclusion. Cependant, le portable permet de chercher un mot dans un dictionnaire en ligne ou de prévenir ses parents. [However, it lets you look up a word or warn parents.] En conclusion, il faut que chaque élève éteigne son téléphone pendant les cours. [In conclusion, each pupil must switch off his phone in lessons.] Éteigne is subjunctive after il faut que.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child writes bien que c'est utile. Correction: bien que ce soit utile, because bien que needs the subjunctive. Another repeats et all the time; vary it with de plus, en outre, par ailleurs. Another writes je pense que ce soit utile. Correction: je pense que c'est utile, because penser que takes the indicative.

Step 6, Your turn: write a two-sentence introduction for Faut-il porter un uniforme à l'école ? Model answer: Dans de nombreux pays, les élèves portent un uniforme. Faut-il pour autant généraliser cette règle ? [In many countries pupils wear a uniform. Should this rule be adopted everywhere?]

Step 1, Prepare to listen and take notes. The title is Un job pour l'été [A summer job]. Write only keywords, not full sentences: who, wants, does, when, advice. Use abbreviations and arrows, for example Inès > job été > argent. You will have about two minutes to write after the second listening.

Step 2, Listen to the dialogue. Read aloud: Inès : Je cherche un petit job pour l'été. Karim : Moi, je fais du bénévolat à la bibliothèque, deux heures par semaine, le mercredi. Inès : C'est gratuit ? Karim : Oui, mais j'apprends beaucoup. Je range les livres et j'aide les enfants à lire. Inès : Je veux gagner un peu d'argent. Karim : Alors essaie le marché : le samedi, ils cherchent quelqu'un.

Step 3, Extract the key points. Inès : cherche un job pour l'été ; veut de l'argent. Karim : bénévole à la bibliothèque ; 2 h par semaine ; mercredi ; range les livres ; conseille le marché, le samedi. Two speakers and two ideas each is enough for a summary.

Step 4, Summarise in your own words. Inès cherche un job pour l'été parce qu'elle veut gagner de l'argent. Karim fait du bénévolat à la bibliothèque le mercredi et il lui conseille de chercher au marché, où l'on cherche quelqu'un le samedi. Use third person and link with parce que and et.

Step 5, Fix errors. A child copies je cherche and je fais. Correction: change to elle cherche and il fait. Another copies the dialogue word for word. Correction: use your own words and keep only the key facts, so the summary is clearly shorter than the dialogue.

Step 6, Your turn: summarise this dialogue. Tom : Je vais au cinéma samedi. Sara : Moi, je dois garder ma petite sœur. Tom : Viens dimanche alors ! Answer: Tom va au cinéma samedi, mais Sara doit garder sa petite sœur ; il lui propose donc de venir dimanche.

Step 1, Choose a topic and plan three parts. Topic: Le métier que je voudrais faire [The job I would like to do]. Parts: introduction (who I am and the topic), development (why, studies, qualities), conclusion (summary and thanks). A two-minute talk at about 100 words per minute is roughly 200 words.

Step 2, Write an opening with a plan. Bonjour à tous. Aujourd'hui, je vais vous parler du métier d'ingénieur en environnement. [Today I am going to talk about the job of environmental engineer.] Je présenterai d'abord pourquoi ce métier m'intéresse, puis les études nécessaires. Announce the plan so listeners can follow.

Step 3, Develop each part with a reason and a detail. D'abord, ce métier m'intéresse parce que je veux protéger la nature. [First, it interests me because I want to protect nature.] Ensuite, il faut faire cinq ans d'études après le lycée, en général. [Then you need about five years of study after lycée, generally.] Vary your connectors.

Step 4, Use keywords and plan for questions. Write only keywords on a card: protéger, études, qualités, merci. After the talk, you may hear a question: Pourriez-vous répéter la question ? [Could you repeat the question?] Practise this and Je voudrais ajouter que... [I would like to add that...].

Step 5, Fix errors. A child says Je vais parler sur le métier. Correction: Je vais parler du métier, because parler de is the construction. Another says il faut que je fais. Correction: il faut que je fasse, subjunctive of faire. Another speaks too fast; pause at each full stop.

Step 6, Your turn: introduce your topic Un sport que j'aime and give a three-part plan in three sentences. Model answer: Bonjour à tous. Aujourd'hui, je vais vous parler du basket, un sport que j'aime. D'abord, je présenterai les règles, puis les bienfaits, enfin mon équipe.

Step 1, Explain Earth's structure and plates. Earth has a core, a mantle and a thin crust. The crust and upper mantle form rigid tectonic plates that move a few centimetres per year. Their movement builds and breaks landforms. Draw a cross-section and label the crust as the thinnest layer, only a small share of Earth's radius.

Step 2, Link plate boundaries to landforms. At a convergent boundary plates collide: the Indian and Eurasian plates created the Himalayas as fold mountains. At a divergent boundary plates separate: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge forms new ocean floor. At a transform boundary plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes along faults such as the San Andreas.

Step 3, Explain weathering, erosion and deposition. Weathering breaks rock where it lies, by frost, heat or rain. Erosion moves material. A river cuts a V-shaped valley near its source, carries sediment and deposits it on a floodplain or in a delta near the sea. Write the three words in order for a mountain stream.

Step 4, Explain climate controls. Latitude: the equator gets the most direct sunlight, because Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees and the tropics lie at 23.5 degrees north and south. Altitude: air cools about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 m. Worked example: 28 degrees at sea level, a station at 3,000 m is 28 - 19.5 = 8.5 degrees.

Step 5, Explain a regional pattern. Near the equator the rising air of the Intertropical Convergence Zone brings heavy rain. In June to August this zone moves north, and in South Asia warm moist winds blow from sea to land, producing the monsoon rains. Dry months follow when winds reverse. Link wind direction to rainfall in two sentences.

Step 6, Your turn: a town at 200 m has 24 degrees Celsius. Estimate the temperature at a village at 2,200 m and name the process. Answer: The height difference is 2,000 m and 2 x 6.5 = 13 degrees, so 24 - 13 = 11 degrees Celsius; temperature falls with altitude at the lapse rate.

Step 1, Describe the oceans. Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth's surface. Average salinity is about 35 parts per thousand, meaning 35 g of salt in 1 kg of seawater. Worked example: 2 kg of seawater holds 2 x 35 = 70 g salt. Salinity is lower where rivers and rain add fresh water and higher in hot, dry seas.

Step 2, Describe surface currents. Winds and Earth's rotation drive large circular systems called gyres. They turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. The Gulf Stream carries warm water north-eastwards across the Atlantic, warming western Europe, while the cold Humboldt (Peru) Current flows north along South America's west coast.

Step 3, Describe deep circulation. Cold, salty water is dense and sinks near the poles, then flows slowly along the ocean floor, while warm surface water moves toward the poles to replace it. This slow conveyor, driven by temperature and salinity, moves heat around the planet and takes centuries to complete a circuit.

Step 4, Describe soil formation. Soil forms from five factors: parent rock, climate, relief, living organisms and time. Rock is weathered into mineral particles, plants add humus, and water moves material downward. A soil profile has an O layer of litter, an A topsoil rich in humus, a B subsoil and a C layer of weathered rock.

Step 5, Link soils and vegetation. In hot, wet regions heavy rain leaches nutrients, leaving red laterite soils but fast-growing rainforest. Temperate grasslands often build deep dark soils rich in humus. Safety for a soil jar test: wear gloves, do not taste or sniff directly, and wash hands afterward. Describe how climate changes soil colour.

Step 6, Your turn: state the gyre direction in the Southern Hemisphere and name the soil horizon holding most humus. Then find the salt in 5 kg of seawater. Answer: anticlockwise; the A horizon (topsoil); 5 x 35 = 175 g of salt.

Step 1, Describe population distribution. World population passed 8 billion in 2022. Density is people divided by area. Worked example: an invented country has 60 million people on 300,000 square kilometres, so density = 60,000,000 / 300,000 = 200 people per square kilometre. Population clusters near rivers, coasts and fertile plains and is sparse in deserts and high mountains.

Step 2, Calculate natural change. Birth rate is births per 1,000 people per year; death rate is deaths per 1,000. If birth rate is 20 and death rate is 8, natural increase is 20 - 8 = 12 per 1,000, which is 1.2 percent. The rule of 70 gives doubling time as 70 / 1.2, about 58 years.

Step 3, Analyse the demographic transition. Stage 1 has high birth and death rates. In stage 2 death rates fall first, so population grows fast. In stage 3 birth rates fall. In stage 4 both are low and growth is slow. Ask which stage a country is in by checking its rates and age structure.

Step 4, Analyse settlement patterns. A nucleated settlement clusters around a centre such as a crossroads. A linear settlement follows a road, river or coast. A dispersed settlement has scattered farms. Site is the exact spot, for example a dry hill above a river, while situation is its position relative to routes and other places.

Step 5, Analyse urbanisation. The world became more than 50 percent urban around 2007. Rural people migrate to cities because of push factors such as low incomes and pull factors such as jobs and schools. Rapid growth can strain housing and water supply. Explain how one pull factor could attract a family.
Step 6, Your turn: a country has birth rate 30 and death rate 10 per 1,000. Find natural increase and doubling time. Answer: 30 - 10 = 20 per 1,000, which is 2 percent; 70 / 2 = 35 years.

Step 1, Read the scale. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground, which is 500 m. Worked example: a path 4.6 cm long is 4.6 x 500 = 2,300 m, or 2.3 km. Check the scale in the key before you measure, because different maps use different scales.

Step 2, Give a six-figure grid reference. Read along the bottom (eastings) first, then up the side (northings): along the corridor, then up the stairs. A church in square 12 across and 34 up, four tenths across and seven tenths up, has reference 124347. Write eastings first every time.

Step 3, Read contours and gradient. Contour lines join places of equal height. Close lines mean a steep slope; wide lines mean a gentle slope. Gradient is vertical rise divided by horizontal distance. If land rises 100 m over 2,000 m, the gradient is 100 / 2,000 = 0.05, or 5 percent, which is 1 in 20.

Step 4, Use simple statistics. Monthly rainfall in mm: 6, 9, 9, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20. Sum = 104, so mean = 104 / 8 = 13. The median is the middle of the ordered list, (12 + 14) / 2 = 13. The mode is 9, the most common. The range is 20 - 6 = 14.

Step 5, Interpret and present data. Use a line graph for change over time, a bar chart for comparing places, a scatter graph for a relationship between two variables. A mean of 13 mm with a range of 14 mm suggests rainfall varies a lot. State the pattern, then give one reason it matters.
Step 6, Your turn: on a 1:25,000 map a road measures 6 cm. How long is it on the ground? Answer: 1 cm is 25,000 cm, which is 250 m, so 6 x 250 = 1,500 m, or 1.5 km.

Step 1, Read a population pyramid. A wide base means many children and high birth rates; a narrow top means few old people. A column-like shape means low birth and death rates. Compare two pyramids by age groups: 0-14, 15-64 and 65 and over. Ask what services each country will need, such as schools or pensions.

Step 2, Calculate the dependency ratio. Dependency ratio = (children 0-14 + people 65 and over) divided by working-age 15-64, multiplied by 100. Worked example: 25 million children and 15 million older people with 60 million working-age: (25 + 15) / 60 x 100 = 66.7. About 67 dependants for every 100 workers.

Step 3, Classify resources. Renewable resources, such as sunlight, wind and well-managed forests, are replaced naturally. Non-renewable resources, such as coal and oil, are used up on human timescales. Carrying capacity is the number of people an area can support with its resources. Discuss whether trade and technology can raise it.

Step 4, Analyse water per person. A widely used guide treats below 1,700 cubic metres per person per year as water stress, below 1,000 as scarcity and below 500 as absolute scarcity. Example: 51 billion cubic metres for 40 million people gives 51,000,000,000 / 40,000,000 = 1,275, so water stress.

Step 5, Add projection. If the 40 million people grow at 1.5 percent a year for 10 years, population becomes 40 x 1.015 to the power 10, about 46.4 million. Water per person becomes 51 billion / 46.4 million, about 1,099 cubic metres, close to scarcity. Explain two ways the country could respond.

Step 6, Your turn: a country has 30 million people and 36 billion cubic metres of renewable water. Calculate water per person and classify it. Answer: 36,000,000,000 / 30,000,000 = 1,200 cubic metres per person per year, which is water stress.
